evidence: Equipment profiles of Premier, including a Sound on Sound feature summarised in search results, describe his working setup from roughly 1998 onward as an Akai MPC60 sequencing sounds held in an Akai S950 sampler. Gang Starr's first album (1989) was made on an E-mu SP-12, so the MPC60 is not his original machine. The exact year he adopted it is not sourced here, and the Sound on Sound piece itself could not be read directly, so this is held at consensus.

earlier.title: MPC60, sixteen pads and a sequencer

trackPair.whatToListenFor: Listen to the drums. Each hit is a single, short, tightly trimmed sound, a kick, a snare, a hat, played from the pads rather than looped as a chunk of someone else's drummer. That is why they sound so punchy and separate. Then listen to the sample on top. It has been cut into small pieces and replayed in a new order, so you hear a phrase you almost recognise that never quite goes where the original did.

explanation: DJ Premier used an MPC60 to control a separate sampler. He cut drum sounds and bits of old records into tiny pieces, put them on the pads, and played them in new patterns: the MPC's pads and sequencer suit chopping short fragments and replaying them in new orders, rather than long loops, and Premier is the clearest example. His drums sound short and punchy, and his samples sound familiar but rearranged, and lots of 1990s New York rap sounds like this because of him. It is held at consensus because the setup is documented in gear profiles of his later work rather than tied to particular sessions.
